articles.title: 99% pure lithium extraction became possible with US scientists’ new electrochemical method
articles.description: Researchers from UChicago PME used electrochemical intercalation to extract 99% pure lithium from a solution where the ratio of sodium to lithium was 1,000 to 1.

articles.title: South Korean team uses brain oxidant to activate Alzheimer’s prodrug
articles.description: KAIST researchers created a prodrug activated by hydrogen peroxide in diseased brains, reducing oxidative stress and amyloid buildup in mice.

articles.title: 'Milestone': Scientists claim to build synthetic cell, raising concerns in step toward artificial life
articles.description: University of Minnesota researchers say "SpudCell" is the most life-like synthetic cell yet, able to grow, divide and pass traits to offspring.

articles.title: Scientists discover a protein switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
articles.description: A protein called “Mitch” may hold the key to a new generation of obesity treatments. Researchers found that disabling it in human cells boosts fat burning, increases energy use, and makes it harder for new fat cells to develop. The findings help explain why mice lacking Mitch were leaner, more athletic, and resistant to obesity.

articles.title: Single ion scans hidden 3D electromagnetic fields to improve quantum chip performance
articles.description: ETH Zurich researchers used a single trapped ion to create 3D electromagnetic field maps, offering a new way to improve quantum computing.

articles.title: Postwar research compact fueled U.S. prosperity for eight decades, argues commentary
articles.description: As the United States celebrates 250 years of independence, Science has published a commentary by Johns Hopkins University President Ron Daniels highlighting the impact of the reimagining of the American university pioneered by Johns Hopkins in the late 19th century—and how the benefits of that shift and the later emergence of the compact between research universities and the federal government have been integral to the nation's success and prosperity.

articles.title: New drone technology uses nature-inspired signals to predict failures before crashes
articles.description: Scientists developed a nature-inspired method that helps drones detect failures before losing control.

articles.title: Nanozymes map nanoparticle routes inside live cells without genetic engineering
articles.description: Nanoparticles are widely used in medicine to deliver drugs, genes or imaging agents to specific parts of the body. Once a nanoparticle reaches a cell, however, many things can happen—it can reach its target, be degraded, interact with proteins that help transport it, or interact with proteins that hinder its transport.

articles.title: This Giant Planet Survived the Death of its Star
articles.description: Some planets can survive when their main sequence stars "die" and evolve into red giants. Astronomers have found several of them. One of them in particular is orbiting extremely close to its star, providing an opportunity to study it with the JWST to determine how it got there.

articles.title: Coral loss may erase up to $3 billion in Hawaiʻi reef recreation by 2100
articles.description: Coral reef decline driven by climate change could cost Hawaiʻi residents between $1.8 billion and $3 billion in lost reef-related activities by 2100, according to a new study published in Ecological Economics. The research projects that these burdens will not fall equally, with lower-income and disadvantaged communities in the state facing disproportionate impacts.

articles.title: Compromise drives shared risky decisions, but biased blame and credit can break teamwork
articles.description: Relationships are all about compromise. From deciding on where to eat dinner with a friend to negotiating chore lists at home, we often experience situations that require some flexibility. But what happens when we must work with others—especially people we don't know—to make a risky decision? That's what Caltech's Dean Mobbs, professor of cognitive neuroscience, and members of his lab set out to explore in a recent study.

articles.title: Diffractive networks enable optical information transfer through random and unknown diffusers
articles.description: The transmission of optical information through random scattering media is a major challenge in optics, biomedical imaging, telecommunications and remote sensing. When light passes through a turbid or diffusive medium, such as biological tissue or a randomly structured optical material, the original image information can be severely distorted, making reliable recovery difficult.

articles.title: How winter conditions shape future jellyfish blooms
articles.description: Marine scientists at the University of Chester have discovered that environmental conditions experienced by jellyfish before winter can have lasting effects on the size and intensity of jellyfish blooms many months later. The study focused on the moon jellyfish, Aurelia aurita, one of the most common jellyfish species found in coastal waters throughout Europe. While the spectacular blooms of adult jellyfish are familiar to many beachgoers, far less is known about the tiny benthic polyp stage that lies hidden beneath the surface.

articles.title: Quantum properties of multimode light observed despite extreme losses
articles.description: Quantum properties of light are extremely delicate. When researchers attempt to measure them, even small losses on the way to a detector can make them invisible, limiting their use outside carefully controlled environments. A collaborative team of researchers involving scientists at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light (MPL) has shown a new way to measure several quantum channels of light at the same time and reveal their entanglement, even when almost all of the light is lost before reaching the detector. The results, recently published in Nature Communications, open new possibilities for scalable quantum technologies.

articles.title: Spider venoms could stop deadly varroa mites killing honey bees
articles.description: Spider venoms contain ingredients that could lead to a new treatment to protect honeybees from the deadly Varroa destructor mite, according to a study led by the University of the Sunshine Coast. Researchers identified components in the venoms of the Tasmanian cave spider and the giant Japanese funnel-web spider that killed the parasitic mites without harming the bees. The study is published in the journal npj Drug Discovery.
